title: Britain's New 'Be Ready' Guide: How to Cope for 72 Hours on Your Own
summary:
Imagine your phone, lights and fridge all stopped working at once. What would your family do for three days? That is the question Britain is now asking everyone, with a new national guide called 'Be Ready.'

The guide explains how to look after yourself for 72 hours during an emergency, whether it is a big storm, a cyberattack that knocks out computers, or another serious disruption. It suggests keeping extra food, water, medicines and a torch at home.

Britain has not tried anything like this for a very long time. The last national preparedness campaign was in 1980, during the Cold War, when the government sent out strange-looking leaflets called 'Protect and Survive.' People laughed at it. This time, officials say they want calm, useful tips, not scary messages.

The head of the British Army, General Sir Roland Walker, told about 700 soldiers last month that the world is in 'extreme jeopardy' and that leaders need to talk honestly with the public about risks. Disaster expert Lucy Easthope, who has helped after emergencies including the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, says the public wants reassurance. 'This is reawakening the idea that it's perfectly survivable,' she said.

Other countries in Europe, including France, Sweden, Norway, Germany, Poland and Ireland, have also updated their emergency advice. Canada has held an emergency preparedness week every year since 1996. Britain, by contrast, has mostly counted on neighbours helping each other through short problems.

Some Britons are still unsure. Family doctor Nyari Matebwe, from Hertfordshire, north of London, said her first reaction was to roll her eyes. But recent suspected hacking attacks on supermarket freezers across Europe, and hoax bomb threats at airports, made her think again. Her teenage daughter is now pushing the family to take the message seriously. Parents' chat groups are buzzing with the same question: how would we cook with no gas or electricity? The guide's answer is simple: a little planning now can make a hard few days much easier.
why_it_matters: Emergencies can happen anywhere, and knowing what to do in advance helps families stay safe and calm instead of scared.

background_read: Emergency preparedness means getting ready before a crisis, so a family can manage on its own until help arrives.
The guide uses 72 hours because most short emergencies, like storms or power cuts, can last a few days.
A cyberattack is an attack on computers or networks that can stop phones, banks or shops from working.
Many countries publish this kind of advice so people know what to do calmly instead of panicking.
